# Protocol revenue: what the protocol keeps and what to report

Source: https://lowob.com/research/protocol-revenue-fees-real-yield-and-what-to-report/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-29 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Report what the protocol keeps, with and without incentives, where it came from and what it cost to get, on one page, monthly, in the same format. TVL is a balance, not revenue; protocol revenue is the fee income retained after suppliers are paid. The SEC's 2026 offering proposal points the same way, asking for token economics and, for larger raises, GAAP financial statements.

Report what the protocol keeps, with and without incentives, where it came from and what it cost to get. One page, monthly, same format every time. TVL is a balance, not revenue, and gross fees are not revenue either: protocol revenue is what is left after suppliers are paid. The evidence on incentives shows why the "without" column matters: after Arbitrum's airdrop, total fees rose while activity per address fell. And in the US, the SEC's 2026 offering proposal would ask issuers for exactly this kind of consistent economic disclosure.

## TVL is a balance, not revenue

In crypto, TVL is reach (see [stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/)). It is a snapshot of money parked, often rented with your own token, and it can leave in an afternoon.

A balance tells you what is sitting there today. It does not tell you what the protocol earns, what it costs to hold, or whether it will be there next month. Reporting TVL as a headline number tells a sophisticated reader that you do not know the difference. Or worse, that you do.

Keep TVL on the page. Just stop leading with it. The same goes for headline valuation: Keyrock's review of 62 airdropped token launches found higher launch FDV correlated with a greater chance of a significant price drop, and one launch carried an estimated $6 million of liquidity against a $13 billion FDV. Neither number is a measure of the business.

## What revenue actually is

Revenue for a protocol is the fee income the protocol or its treasury keeps. Not the fees that pass through on the way to someone else.

| Line | What it is | Who it belongs to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gross fees | Everything users paid to use the protocol | Nobody yet |
| Supplier share | Fees paid out to LPs, lenders, depositors, curators | Them |
| Protocol revenue | What is left, retained by the protocol or treasury | You |

Many decks report line one and call it revenue. Investors read line three. The gap between the two is the first thing they will ask about, so put it on the page before they do. Public analytics dashboards label these lines in different ways, so state your own definitions on the page and check which one a data provider uses before you quote its figure.

If protocol revenue is zero by design, say so and explain the plan. Zero with a reason is a strategy. Zero hidden behind gross fees is a problem waiting for a diligence call.

## Incentive-adjusted everything

Every operating metric gets two columns: with incentives, without.

TVL with and without token rewards. Volume with and without rewards. Active users with and without a campaign running. Fees with and without the subsidised rate.

The evidence shows how far the columns can diverge. Academic analysis of Arbitrum's airdrop found transactions per address fell after the drop even as total daily fees rose; the same study found up to 66% of claimed tokens across nine airdrops went to exchanges in the first transfer. A fee line inflated by a campaign is real money in the period. It is not evidence of next period.

Investors do this calculation themselves. Curators do it before listing you. The only question is whether you show your working or they show theirs. [Community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) applies the same rule to community: measure what remains when the incentive stops.

The "without" column is the business. The gap between the columns is the cost of appearing bigger than the business. Both are useful. Only one is revenue.

> The "without" column is the business. The gap is what it costs to look bigger than you are.

## Retention and concentration

Deposits that arrive are reach. Deposits that stay are the product working.

Report retained deposits at 30 and 90 days, by cohort. A cohort is a month of arrivals. Then split each cohort by source: which integration brought it, which issuer, which campaign. [Issuers, integrations and curators](https://lowob.com/research/issuers-integrations-and-curators/) covers building those channels. This is where you find out which ones delivered money that stayed. It is the protocol version of [net revenue retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/): what a cohort is worth a year after it arrived.

Then concentration. Share of TVL from the top three depositors. If one closed fund is your biggest market, you have a ceiling and a single point of failure in the same row. Their redemption is your drawdown.

Concentration is not shameful early. Hiding it is. Show the number and show the plan for bringing it down.

## The cost side and the treasury

Everything above has a cost. Put it on the same page.

Incentive spend per dollar of TVL that was still there at 90 days. Not per dollar that arrived. Per dollar that stayed. That is your acquisition cost, and it will be higher than you want it to be. The arithmetic is the same as [CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/) in any other business: the cost of the retained customer against the margin they produce, with tokens counted at what they cost the treasury.

Grant money is acquisition cost too. A grant that pays for a deployment on a new chain is a marketing spend with a different name. Count it, in the same currency, in the same table.

Treasury is reported in stablecoin terms. Not in your own token at today's price. Holdings, monthly burn, months of runway. If the treasury is mostly your own token, say what it would be worth at a third of the price, because someone will ask.

## Where disclosure is heading

The one page is not only good practice. US regulators are moving towards asking for something like it. The SEC's proposed Regulation Crypto Assets, published on 18 August 2026, would create offering exemptions for crypto-related investment contracts. The Congressional Research Service's summary describes principles-based disclosure across ten topics, including token economics: supply, pricing, lockups, release schedules and mechanisms for creating or destroying the asset. The larger fundraising route would require financial statements under US GAAP, audited for its top tier, with annual, semiannual and current reports. Comments closed on 20 October 2026 and the rule is not final. This is not legal advice, but a protocol that already publishes a consistent monthly page will find the disclosure work far smaller.

In the EU, MiCA Article 6 bars white papers from making assertions on a token's future value. An APY in marketing sits uncomfortably next to that rule, which is another reason the one page leaves it out.

## What to stop reporting, and the one page

Stop reporting headline TVL on its own. Stop reporting APYs anywhere (see [the user story before the token story](https://lowob.com/research/the-user-story-before-the-token-story/)). Stop counting markets as progress; ten markets with no retained deposits is a maintenance burden, not traction. Stop announcing partnerships that are not live with money in them.

| Section | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue | Gross fees, supplier share, protocol revenue |
| Core metrics | TVL, volume, users and fees, each with and without incentives |
| Retention | Retained deposits at 30 and 90 days, by cohort and source |
| Concentration | Top three depositors' share, and the plan to reduce it |
| Acquisition cost | Incentive and grant spend per dollar of 90-day retained TVL |
| Treasury | Holdings, burn and runway in stablecoin terms |
| Commentary | Three sentences on what changed and why |

Same format every month. A curator reads it to size a listing. An investor reads it to check the business. The community reads it to see whether the team tells the truth when the numbers are down. One page that serves all three is the test of whether the business is real. Build it so someone else can produce it when you are not there (see [build it to run without you](https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/)), and hold it to the standard of [commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/).

## lowob takeaways

- **Three revenue lines.** Gross fees, supplier share and protocol revenue, with your definitions stated.
- **Two columns for everything.** With and without incentives; only the second is the business.
- **Retention, concentration, cost per sticky dollar.** By cohort and source, at 30 and 90 days.
- **Stablecoin treasury, no APYs.** Report runway in stablecoins and drop yields, market counts and unlive partnerships.

Measure incentive and grant spend per dollar of TVL still present at 90 days. Put that number, the three revenue lines and the top-three concentration on one page, and send it to your investors in the same format next month.
